newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Author provides peek into militia movement.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Author provides peek into militia movement.

text.p: As Timothy McVeigh was being condemned to death last month for the worst crime of its kind ever on U.S. soil, a new book hit the shelves offering a glimpse into the militant mindset that may have motivated him.

While Chris Offutt's "The Good Brother" (Simon & Schuster) is fiction, it burns with some of the same anti-government, conspiracy-suspicious fire found smouldering in the militia movements and elsewhere during the national self-examination that followed the April 1995 Oklahoma City bombing.

"I was two years into this book, had done a lot of research and was uncovering what to me was an arcane and obscure world and then all of a sudden this building blows up and I couldn't believe it," he told Reuters.

"All of this work I'd done is suddenly smeared across the newspapers. I even considered changing the whole plot of the book because it seemed inappropriate," the Montana-based writer said of his first novel. He said he looked for a way to drop the project, which he found tough going. "But I stuck with it. I didn't have any choice really."
STORY STARTS IN THE COAL MINES

Offutt, who was born in a speck of a coal mining town in eastern Kentucky's Appalachia, sets off his story there. Its central figure is a young man pushed by the code of the hills to avenge his brother's death by murdering his killer.

In a vivid and richly told tale, the man erases his identity, assumes another and winds up in the mountains of western Montana, where an accident drops him into the company of strangers, a group who mistrust the government to the point of refusing even to apply for driver's licenses.

They are young and old, equipped with enough guns to take over a small country and angry at some of the same things that apparently gnawed at McVeigh, including the actions of government agents at Ruby Ridge, Idaho, in 1992 and the cult compound near Waco, Texas, in 1993, when about 80 people died in a blaze sparked by a government raid on David Koresh and his followers. They cite the U.S. Constitution like scripture and mistrust outsiders, and some spout white supremacism.
Yet not all would act on their convictions with violence. And while Offutt does not seek sympathy for them, he does shine light on how they got where they are.

"One thing about the McVeigh business is that he allegedly ... committed an act of violence in retribution for a perceived act of violence by the government in Waco. And now the death penalty of course is a social act of violence committed against him again in retribution for his act of violence," Offutt said.

"My entire novel proceeds along the same lines. It opens with a murder, a guy is forced into an act of violence. The character in my book, it doesn't work out for him. And it doesn't woork out for McVeigh. It's something that typically does not work out for people," he said.

"Some of McVeigh's defence dealt with the material that he'd been exposed to regarding Waco and some of the literature of this movement. I read the same literature. I saw the same videos ... It's very convincing material. It needs to be recognised as such and taken seriously," Offutt added.

"It's not something that's going to go away. It's radical politics from the right. Thirty years ago the radicals were on the left. Yet essentially they have the same ideals -- freedom and questioning the government."

Offutt said he formed his fiction from heavy research into the militia lifestyle and from what he soaked up from living in Montana -- "an environment where people have a fairly healthy scepticism toward the government and where there's a great sense of personal liberty and independence as a value."

Part of what he wanted to do in the book, he added, was to understand "how people who are patriotic, essentially rural people could get caught up in radical politics ... I think obviously McVeigh is someone who got into that."
